paper.title: Sharp Dichotomies for Regret Minimization in Metric Spaces

unmapped: Arbitrary metric space (X,d), known to the learner; expected payoff 1-Lipschitz
Algorithms access the metric space via oracles (covering / ordering oracles)
Guarantees are instance-specific tractability statements (constant may depend on instance)
settings.definition_quote: The payoff from each arm $x\in X$ is an independent sample from a fixed (time-invariant) distribution with support in $[0,1]$ and expectation $\mu(x)$ such that $|\mu(x)-\mu(y)| \leq d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$.

unmapped: Payoff functions drawn i.i.d. from a Borel measure on [0,1]^X with Lipschitz expected payoff; arbitrary known metric space
settings.definition_quote: a problem instance is specified by a triple $(X,d,\prob)$, where $(X,d)$ is a metric space and $\prob$ is a Borel probability measure on the set $[0,1]^X$ of payoff functions on $X$ ... such that the expected payoff function ... is a Lipschitz function on $(X,d)$. In each round an algorithm is presented with an i.i.d. sample from $\prob$.

settings.name_in_paper: Lipschitz experts problem with double feedback
unmapped: Double feedback: learner bets on one strategy and takes one 'free peek'; payoffs of both are revealed (weaker than full information, stronger than bandit). Mapped to full_information as nearest vocabulary value; results hold under the weaker double feedback.
settings.definition_quote: we define the \emph{double feedback}, where in each round the algorithm selects two strategies: the ``bet" for which it receives the payoff, and the ``free peek". After the round, the payoffs are revealed for both strategies.

unmapped: Each realized payoff function in the support of P is itself Lipschitz on (X,d)
settings.definition_quote: a restricted version of \FFproblem\ in which a problem instance $(X,d,\prob)$ satisfies a further property that each function $f\in \mathtt{support}(\mathbb{P})$ is itself a Lipschitz function on $(X,d)$.

source.label: thm:main-alg
source.quote: Consider a compact well-orderable metric space $(X,d)$. Then: (a) the Lipschitz MAB problem on $(X,d)$ is $f$-tractable for every $f\in\omega(\log t)$; (b) the Lipschitz experts problem on $(X,d)$ is 1-tractable, even with a double feedback.

results.notes: Also stated as the upper half of Theorem 1.2. The algorithm depends on f. Needs covering and ordering oracles.

conditions: metric space has a perfect subspace (equivalently, for compact completion: completion uncountable)

source.label: thm:lower-bound
source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz experts problem on a metric space $(X,d)$ which has a perfect subspace. Then the problem is not $g$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$. In fact, ... there exist a distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over problem instances $\mu$ such that for any experts algorithm \A\ we have $\Pr_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}}[ R_{(\A,\,\mu)}(t) = O_{\mu}(g(t)) ] = 0$.

results.notes: Instance-specific statement: for almost every instance from P, regret is not O(g) for any g=o(sqrt t) (an infinitely-often lower bound). Full feedback, hence also applies to bandit (Theorem 1.2 lower half, Theorem 1.4 lower half).

conditions: completion of X is not a compact metric space with countably many points

source.label: thm:main-MAB
source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz MAB problem on a fixed metric space $(X,d)$. Then the following dichotomy holds: either the problem is $f(t)$-tractable for every $f\in \omega(\log t)$, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$. In fact, the former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space with countably many points.

results.notes: Meaning: no algorithm has regret O_I(g(t)) on all instances for g in o(sqrt t); recorded as Omega(sqrt T) instance-specific.

conditions: X is an infinite metric space

source.label: thm:logT
source.quote: For every infinite metric space $(X,d)$, the Lipschitz MAB problem on $(X,d)$ is not $(\log t)$-tractable.

results.notes: Statement is that regret is not O_I(log t) for some instance, i.e. strictly superlogarithmic; Omega(log T) notation understates it.

symbols.eps_t: eps(t) = min{2^{-k}: t <= s_k}, s_k = sum of phase lengths; eps_t -> 0 so regret is o(T)

tuning: phase lengths t_i = min(t*_i, t*_{i+1}, 2 sum_{j<i} t_j) tuned to covering numbers

source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz MAB problem on a compact and complete metric space $(X,d)$. Then $R_\A(t) \leq 5\, \eps(t)\, t$, where $\eps(t) = \min\{ 2^{-k}:\, t\leq s_k\}$ and $s_k = \sum_{i=1}^k\, t_i$. In particular, $R_\A(t) = o(t)$.

results.notes: Gives the upper half of Theorem 1.5 (o(t)-tractability in bandit setting when the completion is compact).

conditions: completion of X is not compact

source.label: thm:boundary-of-tractability
source.quote: The Lipschitz experts problem on a fixed metric space $(X,d)$ is either $f(t)$-tractable for some $f\in o(t)$, even in the bandit setting, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(t)$, even with full feedback. The former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space.

results.notes: Proved in Lemma 7.2: almost surely over a random instance, regret is not O(g) for any g in o(t). Holds with full feedback, hence also for bandit.

symbols.b_lcd: any b > LCD(X), the log-covering dimension of the metric space

tuning: algorithm parameter b; delta = T^{-1/(b+2)} in phase of length T

source.label: thm:ffproblem-naive
source.quote: Consider the \FFproblem\ on a metric space $(X,d)$. For each $b>\LCD(X)$, algorithm $\NaiveExp(b)$ achieves regret $R(t) = O(t^{1-1/(b+2)})$.

results.notes: Constant may depend on the instance/metric space ('for any sufficiently large T'); marked worst_case loosely.

source.label: thm:ulproblem-naive
source.quote: Consider the \ULproblem\ with full feedback. Fix a metric space $(X,d)$. For each $b>\LCD(X)$ such that $b\geq 2$, $\NaiveExp(b-2)$ achieves regret $R(t) = O(t^{1-1/b})$.

source.label: thm:experts-MaxMinLCD-body
source.quote: Fix a metric space $(X,d)$ and let $b=\MaxMinLCD(X)$. The \FFproblem\ on $(X,d)$ is $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma> \tfrac{b+1}{b+2}$, and not $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma < \tfrac{b-1}{b}$.

results.notes: Same as Theorem 1.6. Upper bound proof only sketched; uses depth and covering oracles; Lemma 9.6 stated for compact spaces.
Paper states the lower bound holds even for the uniformly Lipschitz experts problem, so it applies to the general full-feedback problem too.

source.label: thm:experts-MaxMinLCD-unif-body
source.quote: Consider the \ULproblem\ with full feedback. Fix a metric space $(X,d)$ with uncountably many points, and let $b=\MaxMinLCD(X)$. The problem on $(X,d)$ is $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma> \max(\tfrac{b-1}{b},\, \tfrac12)$, and not $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma < \max(\tfrac{b-1}{b},\, \tfrac12)$.

results.notes: Same as Theorem 1.7. Upper bound proof only sketched.
